title: Course outline
text:
Week
Topics
Lessons
Activities




Week 1-2
Foundation of academic writing

Overview of academic writing genres and their purposes.
Discussion of the key principles of academic writing.
Introduction to the structure of academic papers.




Week 3-4
Developing research methods

Formulating research topics and research questions.
Identifying relevant literature and conducting a literature review.
Developing a thesis statement and creating an outline for a research paper.




Week 5-6
Writing first darf

Writing effective introductions and conclusions.
Crafting clear and concise methods and results section.
Writing persuasive literature and discussions.
Using appropriate language and tone in academic writing.




Week 7-8
Revising and editing

Strategies for revising and editing academic writing.
Peer review and feedback exercises.
Using tools and resources for editing and proofreading.




Week 9-10
Navigating peer-review process

Overview of the peer-review process in academic publishing.
Selecting appropriate journals for submission.
Preparing manuscripts for submission.
Responding to reviewer feedback and revising manuscripts.




Week 11-12
Ethical considerations in publishing

Discussion of plagiarism, authorship, and other ethical issues in academic publishing.
Introduction to copyright and intellectual property.
Exploration of open access and alternative publishing models.




Week 13-14
Conference presentation and other scholarly outputs

Preparing and delivering effective conference presentations.
Writing conference abstracts and proposal.
Exploring other scholarly outputs.




Week 15-16
Final project presentations and discussion

Presentation of final research papers and other scholarly projects.
Discussion and feedback from peers and instructor.
Reflections on the course and future goals in academic writing and publishing.

title: Econ 148: Analytical and statistical packages for economics 1
text:
Class schedule: Friday | 10:00 - 12:00  Laboratory schedule: Friday | 13:00 - 16:00  Instructor: Christopher Llones  e-mail: christopher.llones@vsu.edu.ph  Pre-requisites: Econ 106 - Computer programming for Economics  Course credits: 3 units  Number of hours: 2 hrs lectures and 3 hrs laboratory per week 


Course description
This course introduces undergraduate students to the use of analytical and statistical packages in economics, with a focus on R programming. It provides hands‑on training in data management, visualization, and basic econometric analysis. Students will learn how to design surveys, handle datasets, test hypotheses, and build regression models, while producing clear and reproducible reports for academic and applied economic contexts.


Course objectives
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

Use R and RStudio for economic data analysis.
Design and manage survey data, including creating questionnaires and codebooks.
Clean, transform, and organize datasets using Tidyverse functions.
Create effective visualizations with ggplot2 to present economic data clearly.
Apply hypothesis testing to evaluate economic questions using parametric and non‑parametric methods.
Perform correlation and regression analysis to explore relationships among economic variables.
Model binary outcomes using probability models such as Logit and Probit.
Prepare reproducible reports with Quarto, integrating code, results, and interpretation for academic assignments.



Course outline








Topics
Lessons
Description




Module 1: Introduction to Statistical Methods

Basics of statistical concept
Questionnaire design
Encoding survey responses
Cleaning and preparing datasets


Understand variables, data types, and measures of central tendency (mean, median) and variability (standard deviation, variance).
Create valid and reliable survey instruments for collecting economic and social data.
Learn proper coding and data entry practices to ensure accuracy and consistency in datasets.
Detect errors, handle missing values, and organize raw survey data into structured formats ready for analysis.



Module 2: Exploring and generalizing data

Frequencies and distribution
Summary statistics
Data visualization


Use histograms and density plots to visualize how often specific values occur in a dataset
Calculate measures of central tendency (mean, median) and spread (standard deviation, variance)
Apply professional guidelines for usage, encoding, and scaffolding to produce informative graphs.



Module 3: Comparison and correlations

Conditional statistics
Association


Compare the distribution and mean of an outcome variable across different values of a conditioning variable.
Measure mean-dependence between variable using covariance and correlation coefficient..



Module 4: Testing hypotheses

Logic of testing
Decision-making
Errors
Multiple testing


Use data evidence to decide if a statement about a population or general pattern is likely true or false.
Apply t-tests and compare p-values against significance level to reject or maintain a null hypothesis.
Distinguish between false positive (rejecting a true null) and false negatives (failing to reject a false null)
Recognize the risk of “p-hacking” and false positives when testing many hypotheses simultaneously.



Module 5: Regression analysis

Simple regression
Inderence for coefficients
Multiple regression
Categorical predictors
Interactions


Model mean-dependence between independent and dependent variable using best-fitting OLS line.
Calculate expected values and use residuals to identify observations that deviate from general pattern.
Compare average y across x values while controlling for other variables (covariates) to reduce bias.
Include qualitative categories in regressions by transforming them into a series of binary dummy variables.
Uncover how the relationship between y and x varies across different groups or values of a third variable.
